newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik government agrees ceasefire with guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: Tajik government agrees ceasefire with guerrillas.

text.p: The Tajik government and its Islamist opponents fighting a bitter civil war agreed to a ceasefire from midnight on Wednesday, but violence continued to overshadow the troubled former Soviet republic.

The U.N. special envoy to Tajikistan expressed satisfaction with peace talks, but previous ceasefire agreements have been routinely flouted. A U.N.-sponsored ceasefire reconfirmed in July began to collapse almost as soon as it was signed.
President Imamali Rakhmonov and Islamic opposition leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri agreed to the truce during talks in neighbouring Afghanistan.
"Both sides have agreed to cease hostilities from midnight (1900 GMT) tonight," Zafar Saidov, spokesman for Rakhmonov, told Reuters by telephone in the Tajik capital Dushanbe.
Saidov said the deal would last at least until December 19 when Rakhmonov and Nuri are expected to meet in Moscow to sign a peace agreement.
No details have been given on the proposed accord but an aide to Nuri, cited by Russia's Interfax news agency on Tuesday, said some form of a coalition government was being considered.
Saidov said opposition fighters had agreed to withdraw from the towns of Komsomolabad, Tajikabad and Jirgadal in the east of the country.
"The president believes the ceasefire is a big achievement," Saidov said.

The United Nations special envoy to Tajikistan, Gerd Merrem, cited by Russia's Interfax news agency, said U.N. military observers based in Tajikistan were ready to fan out in areas of recent fighting to check both sides were holding the ceasefire.
U.N. military observers were withdrawn from the region earlier this month after two of their number were beaten and subjected to a mock execution by government troops.
Merrem, present at the negotiations in Afghanistan, was quoted by the agency as saying that the talks were "more than satisfactory".
Fighting flared in the former Soviet republic after the talks were announced last month as each side tried to improve their hand at the negotiating table.
In a separate development, the Tajik interior ministry said a Russian serviceman based in Dushanbe was shot dead on his way home late on Tuesday.

The killing follows a spate of attacks, widely blamed on the opposition, against Russian troops, thousands of whom fulfil peacekeeping duties, guard the country's southern border with Afghanistan and help shore up Rakhmonov's shaky government.
The opposition has never formally claimed responsibility for the attacks on Russian servicemen in Tajikistan.

The four-year civil war has left tens of thousands dead and made many more homeless in the remote, mountainous country where regional and clan rivalries underlie the conflict between the secular government and Islamist guerrillas.
